question: Inherited hyperammonemia is a result of deficiency of which enzyme of Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "N-acetyl glutamate synthetase deficiency" -> "decreased N-acetylglutamate" -> "reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I" -> "impaired urea cycle" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Malate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Isocitrate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Succinate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
analysis: Inherited hyperammonemia is a condition resulting from the accumulation of ammonia in the blood due to defects in the urea cycle. The urea cycle is responsible for converting toxic ammonia into urea, which can then be excreted from the body. N-acetyl glutamate synthetase is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in the urea cycle by producing N-acetylglutamate, an essential activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme in the urea cycle. A deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase leads to reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, impairing the urea cycle and causing ammonia to accumulate, resulting in hyperammonemia. The other enzymes listed (malate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and succinate dehydrogenase) are part of the Krebs cycle, which is not directly involved in ammonia detoxification. Therefore, the most likely correct answer is that a deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase can lead to inherited hyperammonemia.
